claims.text: Dynamic formation and modulation of surface-bound Pt–OH species governs catalytic activity in ethanol oxidation.
Dynamic Pt–OH coverage governs ethanol-oxidation selectivity.
Dynamic Pt–OH coverage governs catalyst durability during ethanol oxidation.
Pt–OH groups produce balanced adsorption strengths for reaction intermediates.
Balanced intermediate adsorption facilitated by Pt–OH promotes proton-coupled electron transfer.
The representative PGM high-entropy nanoscale catalyst can catalyze ethanol oxidation through a 12-electron process.
The ethanol-oxidation process involves 12 proton transfers.
The catalyst is operated under standard low-temperature fuel-cell conditions.
Changing electrolyte pH systematically changes local hydroxyl coverage on the catalyst.
Introducing a competitive OH− adsorption inhibitor reduces Pt–OH coverage.
Surface-bound Pt–OH species alter the electronic configuration of active sites.
Pt–OH species form on the catalyst surface under ethanol-oxidation conditions.
An optimal Pt–OH coverage promotes a balanced adsorption–desorption equilibrium and improves management of multiple charge-transfer steps.
A controlled initial increase in OH− coverage should increase ethanol-oxidation activity by stabilizing key intermediates.
A controlled initial increase in OH− coverage should enhance ethanol-oxidation selectivity.
Excessive OH− coverage can block sites and reduce catalytic effectiveness.
Suppressing Pt–OH formation through lower pH or an inhibitor should diminish catalytic performance.
The proposed mechanism applies when ethanol oxidation is dominated by proton-coupled electron transfer.
The mechanism may fail when non-PCET pathways dominate.
Extreme pH can fundamentally alter surface speciation and invalidate the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The baseline contains no OH− inhibitor, yet reduced inhibitor concentration is proposed as a way to increase OH− coverage; inhibitor concentration cannot be reduced relative to that stated baseline.
